--------------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen design:  Country-sector panel, staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study (Sun & Abraham 2021 “interaction-weighted” estimator).

Rationale  
•  The reform episode is discrete and well-dated (trade- and FDI-policy liberalisations).  
•  Countries adopt at different calendar years, giving staggered timing that can be exploited.  
•  We observe multiple pre- and post-reform years, so we can check dynamic effects and pre-trends.  
•  Sector-level outcomes allow us to difference out unobserved country-wide shocks with country-year fixed effects and sector-specific global shocks with sector-year fixed effects, tightening the design.  

Optional extension (reported in robustness section): Instrument inward FDI with “gravity-style predicted FDI” based on partner-country growth and distance to address simultaneity between FDI inflows and outcomes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TREAT_icst = 1 if country c has implemented a liberalisation episode by year t and sector s is “exposed”.  
Two operationalisations:

(A) Binary treatment (baseline):  
•  TREAT_ct = 1 starting the first full year after a major national policy package that:  
   – Reduces average MFN tariffs by ≥25% and/or  
   – Removes equity caps on foreign ownership in ≥50% of manufacturing sectors.  
•  For sectors, we simply assign the country-level indicator (all sectors treated simultaneously).

(B) Continuous exposure (robustness):  
•  ΔTariff_cst = pre-post percentage-point drop in sector-specific tariff.  
•  ΔFDIpolicy_ct = 1 if the sector is newly opened to 100% foreign equity.

Control group / counterfactual  
Country-sectors that ­have not yet liberalised in year t (including never-liberalisers) serve as contemporaneous controls.  
Because reforms are staggered, the same country-sector can be control pre-reform and treated post-reform (“not-yet-treated” comparator design).

Treatment timing / event date  
event_year_ct = first year in which TREAT_ct = 1. The event study will create leads and lags k = −6,…,+10 relative to this date.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends  
Absent the policy, treated and not-yet-treated country-sectors would have evolved along parallel productivity and growth paths.  
Plausibility: Reasonable after saturating the regression with (i) country×sector fixed effects, (ii) country×year fixed effects, and (iii) sector×year fixed effects. Nevertheless must be tested by pre-trend coefficients in the event study.

A2. No anticipation / limited anticipation  
Firms do not strongly adjust outcomes more than, say, two years before official implementation.  
Plausibility: Large-scale legislative packages are often announced within months of implementation, but multiyear WTO accession negotiations could invalidate it. We will include leads up to six years to detect anticipatory effects.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA)  
The liberalisation status of one country does not directly change industrial outcomes in another except through common shocks already netted out by year fixed effects.  
Plausibility: Some spillovers (trade diversion) possible; mitigated in robustness by dropping countries that are more than 10% of regional GDP.

A4. Exogeneity of reform timing after conditioning on covariates  
Political cycles or crises that co-determine timing would bias estimates if they also affect industry outcomes. We will control for elections, IMF programmes, and commodity-price shocks at the country-year level.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Non-parallel pre-trends  
   •  Test: Plot and jointly test the estimated lead coefficients (k = −6…−2).  
   •  Remedy:  (i) Include country-specific linear and quadratic trends, (ii) match on pre-reform growth rates, (iii) implement synthetic-control-style weighting as robustness.

2. Confounding simultaneous reforms (e.g., privatisation, macro-stabilisation)  
   •  Control variables: binary indicators for major structural reforms (privatisation index, macro-stabilisation episodes, IMF programmes).  
   •  Triple-difference on sector exposure: Interact treatment with initial tariff level to difference out country-level confounders.

3. Endogenous FDI inflows  
   •  IV robustness: Predict FDI using standard gravity variables (distance-weighted global GDP growth of partner countries, bilateral BIT network). Use the predicted FDI inflow as instrument for observed FDI when estimating its impact on productivity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 5. R CODE OUTLINE
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # fast high-dimensional FE regressions
library(did2s)         # Sun & Abraham implementation
library(ivreg)         # IV robustness

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("country_sector_panel.csv")   # assume wide format

# 2. Variable construction ------------------------------------------
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(event_year = ifelse(policy_start_year > 0, policy_start_year, NA),
         rel_year   = year - event_year,                      # event time
         treat      = if_else(year >= policy_start_year & !is.na(policy_start_year), 1, 0),
         pre_period = if_else(rel_year < 0, 1, 0),
         post_period= if_else(rel_year >=0,1,0))

# Collapse leads/lags beyond window
max.lead  <- -6
max.lag   <- 10
df <- df %>% 
  mutate(rel_year_clipped = pmax(pmin(rel_year, max.lag), max.lead))

# 3. Baseline Sun & Abraham DID -------------------------------------
# Sun & Abraham via did2s (two-stage frist-differences approach)
event_spec <- feols(
  log_prod ~ sunab(policy_start_year, year) | 
            country + sector + country^year + sector^year,
  data = df, cluster = ~country)

summary(event_spec)

# 4. Main parametric DID (average post effect) ----------------------
avg_did <- feols(
  log_prod ~ treat | country+sector+country^year+sector^year,
  data = df, cluster = ~country)

summary(avg_did)

# 5. Robustness: add country-specific linear trend ------------------
avg_did_trend <- feols(
  log_prod ~ treat | country + sector + country^year + sector^year + country[trend],
  data = df, cluster = ~country)

# 6. Robustness: IV for FDI channel ---------------------------------
iv_spec <- ivreg(
  log_prod ~ treat + log_fdi | . -log_fdi + log_pred_fdi,
  data = df)
clustered_se <- sandwich::vcovCL(iv_spec, cluster = df$country)
coeftest(iv_spec, vcov.=clustered_se)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 6. EXPECTED RESULTS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts positive effects:  
•  Trade liberalisation lowers input costs and increases competitive pressure, raising total factor productivity (TFP). Meta-studies suggest +3 – 8 % in TFP over five years.  
•  FDI liberalisation brings capital and know-how; typical estimates show +5 – 10 % higher labour productivity in receiving sectors.  
Therefore I expect the average treated country-sector to see TFP rise by ≈ 5 % within three years and ≈ 8 – 10 % within ten years, and overall industrial value-added growth accelerate by ≈ 1 pp annually.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Clear, well-dated intervention .................................... 1  
C2: Parallel trends supported by visual / statistical tests ........... 0.5  (must be verified)  
C3: No interference / spillovers ...................................... 0.5  
C4: No time-varying confounders unaccounted for ....................... 0.5  
C5: Robust standard errors and multiple specifications ................ 1  
Overall score ......................................................... 3.5 / 5

--------------------------------------------------------------------
End of empirical research plan
--------------------------------------------------------------------
